fake_nulls.description: Spellings of 'no value' that arrive as text. Observed in real filings; a value equal to one of these is missing, not a value.

person_titles.description: Titles that come before a name. A name part that is only a title is a filer putting MRS in the surname box.

legal_forms.description: Legal forms split off the end of an organisation name to give name_core. Longest first: the order is load-bearing.

leading_articles.description: Articles dropped from the start of a name.

placeholder_numbers.description: Registration numbers that are not one company's identity, so a match key must not merge on them. Three kinds: typed-in placeholders such as '00000000'; words in the number box such as 'ENGLAND' or 'TBA'; and real numbers belonging to formation agents, which appear under dozens of unrelated filed names.
placeholder_numbers._measured: The last two kinds were measured on the full 2026-09-18 snapshot — every value used by ten or more distinct filed names that `fake_nulls` does not already catch. The biggest are 09361466 and 9361466 (45 filed names between them, 4,260 records), 07168188 (23 names, 2,738), SO303142 (12 names, 2,195) and CHE-108.562.489 (12 names, 2,164).

junk_postcodes.description: Postcodes that belong to formation agents' and filing agents' offices rather than to anywhere a person lives, so an address key must not merge on them.
junk_postcodes._measured: Every postcode used by more than 5,000 records per 7.5 million individuals, which is 9,281 of the full snapshot's 13,921,888 person records. Rebuilt from the full 2026-09-18 snapshot, where an earlier 1/32 sample had found 18: 6 added, 4 dropped, 20 in all.

nicknames.description: Diminutives that point at one canonical forename. CHRIS and ALEX are deliberately absent because they do not tell you the gender.

nationalities.description: Nationality, home nations collapsed to BRITISH.

residences.description: Country of residence, home nations collapsed to UK.

countries.description: Country of registration as a short code. This map is for organisations only; people have their own country map, on purpose.

roman_numerals.description: Roman numerals as digits, so FUND II and FUND 2 carry the same suffix. Passthrough, because a suffix that is already a number stays one.

match_keys.name: Person: name and date of birth
match_keys.description: Surname, canonical forename and both parts of the date of birth, with none of them missing. The corroborating columns are the split: a group this size that shares no address and no company is several people with one name, not one person.

match_keys.name: Organisation: country and registration number
match_keys.description: The registration number names the company itself, so with the country it is the strongest key there is. Placeholder numbers are blocked, and a number carrying more than three different names is a formation agent's, not a company's.

match_keys.name: Organisation: core name and type
match_keys.description: For the records the number could not key. Raw name prefixes once collapsed 1,800 unrelated trusts, so the whole core name and the type bucket are the empirically safe key.

vetoes.description: Birth years more than one year apart are different people, whatever the name and address say.
vetoes._measured: Birth years more than one year apart are different people. The 500,000-record sample accepted SABELO SHONGWE born 1958-07 against SABELO SHONGWE born 1995-07 at p = 1.000000: a birth-year disagreement cost 0.23 bits against a postcode worth 12.82 and a surname worth 10.27, so the score could never express it. One year of slack is left for an off-by-one filing.

vetoes.description: Two clearly different forenames at one address are siblings or spouses, not one person. Send to review, because a nickname can look different.
vetoes._measured: Two clearly different forenames are siblings or spouses at one address, not one person. Review and not reject: a filing may carry a middle name where another carries a first name, and the nickname lookup has already had its chance, so a human decides.

vetoes.description: Two clearly different surnames, and nothing else says these are one person: the full postcodes do not agree and neither do the middle names.
vetoes.reason: Surnames {left} and {right}, with no shared postcode or middle name
vetoes._measured: Blocking route pb5 pairs two people who share a forename sound and a date of birth and do NOT share a surname sound. It exists to catch a surname changed at marriage, and at full scale it is what joins strangers: 848,976 of the 6,390,630 accepted person pairs had two different surnames, and nineteen of the twenty largest proposed person entities were built from them. The threshold is 0.85 Jaro-Winkler on the cleaned surname, read off the full run: among accepted pairs with different surnames the share that also agree on a middle name is 29.1% at 0.95 and over, 20.1% from 0.90 to 0.95 and 18.6% from 0.85 to 0.90, then falls to 11.3% from 0.80 to 0.85 and 4.6% from 0.70 to 0.80 — against 42.8% for an accepted pair whose surnames match. Below 0.85 the surname difference stops behaving like a spelling variant. This rule hits 638,883 accepted pairs and rejects them. It removes no accepted pair whose surname and whose full date of birth both agree, because it cannot fire on one.

vetoes.description: Two clearly different surnames are never joined without a person looking, even when the address or the middle name agrees.
vetoes._measured: A surname changed at marriage is a real merge and almost always keeps the address, so v3 leaves it alone. It must still not be made without a person: this rule caps every clearly-different-surname pair at review, so 70,224 accepted pairs that v3 spares — the ones the full postcode or the middle name corroborates — go to a reviewer instead of being merged in silence. Review and not reject, because the corroboration is real evidence and a human can read it.

vetoes.description: Two clearly different middle names, two different birth months and no shared postcode: these are two people with the same first and last name.
vetoes.reason: Middle names {left} and {right}, born in different months and at different addresses
vetoes._measured: The second family of bad merges keeps the surname and changes everything else: Kenneth John Cowan of Suffolk born March 1971 was accepted against Kenneth Gordon Cowan of Ayrshire born November 1972 at p = 0.9636, and Jason James Wignall of Devon born October 1986 against Jason David Wignall of Lancashire born June 1986 at p = 0.9967. Both middle names are filed, both are plainly different, the birth months differ and the addresses are hundreds of miles apart. The 0.7 threshold is v2's, so 'clearly different' means the same thing for a forename and for a middle name; JOHN against JOHN PAUL scores 0.91 and is not touched. This rule hits 157,640 accepted pairs, 82,220 of which no other rule catches. It needs both middle names to be present, so a filing that carries one and not the other is left alone.

vetoes.description: A different birth year and a different birth month are two different dates of birth, not one date filed twice.
vetoes.reason: Born {left} and {right}, and not in the same month
vetoes._measured: v1 leaves one year of slack for an off-by-one filing. This rule says the slack was for a slip, and a birth month that also differs shows it was not a slip: two independent errors in one date is not how a register goes wrong. It hits 279,652 accepted pairs, 204,148 of which no other rule catches — Kirsten Cherie Walker of SG11, a New Zealander born April 1974, was accepted against Kirsten Walker of RH20, British, born February 1973, and neither v3 nor v5 can see it, because the surname matches and only one side filed a middle name. The cost is 11,190 pairs that share a full postcode, where a genuine misfiling would show; they are rejected too, because a filed date of birth is the register's identity field and two of them are two people.

vetoes.description: Two different registration numbers are two registrations.
vetoes._measured: Two different registration numbers, both present, are two registrations. deduping's corporate veto set, ported.

vetoes.description: Fund II is not Fund III: a different number at the end of the name is a different entity.
vetoes._measured: Fund II is not Fund III (deduping's veto B), over the cleaned numeric suffix with roman numerals read as digits.

_vetoes_measured_and_not_shipped.why_not: It hits 86,802 pairs on the 500,000-record sample, 10,509 of which the run would otherwise have accepted, and the accepted ones look like one person rather than two: Mr Talat Mahmood BRITISH against Mr Talat Mahmood Pakistani, Mrs Selina Nyasha Bota Zimbabwean against Mrs Selina Nyasha Chimwara BRITISH. Naturalisation and a married name both change the filing, so a nationality disagreement is not evidence of two people. nationality_norm also holds comma-joined multi-values ('British,Cypriot'), which `differs` reads as one string.

deduping's veto D. It hits 509 pairs, 506 of which the run would otherwise have accepted, and 503 of the 509 carry the SAME registration number. Every example is one company filed twice with the country misspelt: UK against UNITED KINGDSOM, ENGALND, UNITIED KINGDOM, UNITED KINGDOM ENGLAND AND WALES COMPANIES HOUSE. country_canonical carries 435 distinct values where it should carry about 200 codes, because the `countries` lookup is fallback: passthrough and leaves a misspelling as it found it. Turn this on once that lookup covers the spellings, or once its fallback is null.

deduping's veto A. It hits 104 pairs, 79 of which the run would otherwise have accepted, and every example is one form spelled two ways: LIMITED against LTD, HOLDINGS LIMITED against GROUP HOLDINGS LIMITED. legal_form_clean is the raw token strip_tokens took off the end, not a canonical form, and the sample holds 139 of them (LIMITED 14,175, LTD 4,819, HOLDINGS LIMITED 3,123, GROUP LIMITED 1,857). What is missing is a `legal_form` lookup mapping those spellings onto a canonical form, the same shape as deduping's has_*_suffix priority ladder. Turn this on against that column, not this one.
